name: Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups
title: Support for Tutors and Intervention Groups
answer: AI can support mathematics learning by coaching the adults who teach it, especially tutors and intervention groups. In a large trial, students of novice tutors who received an AI assistant were more likely to master topics, with the weakest tutors seeing the largest gains. The idea matters because it improves instruction without replacing the tutor's judgment.

sections.body: This idea is about using AI to help tutors and teachers who run intervention groups, rather than putting AI directly in front of students. It solves the problem of novice tutors and busy teachers lacking the time and expertise to plan effective sessions. The AI suggests what to say next or drafts lesson plans, but the adult remains the decision maker. The approach treats the tool as a coach for the tutor, and the tutor as the teacher of the child. It also helps districts choose tutoring services or train volunteers by looking for tools that support rather than replace the tutor.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a tutor can receive a short AI-generated brief summarizing what a student is working on and where they struggle, so the session starts faster. The tutor reads the brief, adjusts it, and brings their own judgment to the session. For intervention groups, a teacher can use data from Zearn or Khan Academy to plan groups, then ask an AI tool to draft a short lesson for each group. The teacher adjusts the plan based on what they know about the students. The time saved goes back into the small group lessons themselves. The text does not give separate grade band examples beyond the kindergarten through twelfth grade mathematics context.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this as some of the best evidence for AI in math. It cites a large trial in a Southern US school district with novice tutors working with 1,800 students, where an AI assistant suggested what to say next (Wang et al., 2024). Students of tutors with access were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics, and students of the weakest tutors gained 9 points. The study used a research tool rather than a commercial product, but the idea can guide district choices.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. The tool coached the tutor, and the tutor taught the child, so the adult keeps the judgment and the relationship. The study used a research tool, not a commercial product, so districts should look for tools that support the tutor rather than replace them. A short brief for each tutor can help, but the tutor reads it, adjusts it, and brings their own judgment to the session. For intervention groups, the teacher adjusts the AI-drafted plan based on what they know about the students. The decisions about what to teach and how to adapt stay with the person.
